result: In AKAP450/CAMSAP2 double knockout RPE1 cells treated with centrinone B for 11 days to remove centrioles, a single compact acentriolar MTOC (caMTOC) forms that generates a dense radial microtubule array. These caMTOCs are cylindrical in ~35% of cells and round in ~38% of cells, consisting of small clusters of PCM components including pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, ninein and dynein.
evaluation: Claims C7, C8, C49-C56, C61-C65 collectively demonstrate the formation of caMTOCs through multiple lines of evidence including immunofluorescence microscopy (Figures 1C-F), quantification of cell populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and STED microscopy analysis (Figure 1F-G). The data show consistent formation of these structures across different experimental approaches.

result: Interphase caMTOC formation requires pericentrin, γ-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, ninein, and dynein, but not CEP152, CEP192, or NEDD1. Depletion of pericentrin, γ-tubulin, CDK5RAP2, or ninein prevents caMTOC coalescence, while depletion of dynein prevents any PCM clustering. CEP152, CEP192, and NEDD1 are neither enriched in caMTOCs nor required for their formation.
evaluation: Claims C9-C15 and C79-C94 are supported by systematic siRNA depletion experiments (Figures 2A-K) showing differential requirements for PCM proteins. The data include both immunofluorescence localization and functional depletion studies with quantification. Western blots confirm protein expression levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B), and knockout cell lines validate the pericentrin requirement (Figures 2E, J).

result: caMTOCs strongly affect microtubule network organization and density in acentriolar cells. Cells lacking pericentrin, dynein, or γ-tubulin show the strongest loss of microtubule density and ~46% non-radial microtubules, while depletion of CDK5RAP2 or ninein produces milder phenotypes with 25-30% non-radial microtubules. Control cells with caMTOCs have only ~12% non-radial microtubules.
evaluation: Claims C97-C105 are supported by quantitative analysis of microtubule organization using radiality mapping (Figures 3A-E). The data show statistically significant differences (p<0.001) between conditions, with appropriate controls and multiple measurements (n=25-56 cells per condition). The conclusion that PCM clustering promotes dense microtubule organization follows logically from the data.

result: caMTOCs fragment into small clusters upon nocodazole treatment at 37°C and reassemble after washout, with both processes driven by dynein activity. During partial microtubule depolymerization, PCM clusters move rapidly (up to 2 μm/s) along minus-end-out microtubules. When microtubules are depolymerized by cold treatment, caMTOCs remain intact, indicating PCM self-association is sufficient for stability but microtubules shape the cluster.
evaluation: Claims C106-C126 are supported by multiple experimental approaches including immunofluorescence (Figures 4A-C, I), live cell imaging (Figures 4E-F), motor-PAINT analysis (Figure 4G), and dynein inhibitor experiments (Figures 4A-D). The data consistently show dynein-dependent dynamics and provide mechanistic insight through quantification of PCM cluster velocities and microtubule orientations.

result: After nocodazole washout, small PCM clusters positive for pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, and PCM1 appear within 30 seconds at microtubule plus-ends and coalesce through microtubule-based movements to form a single caMTOC within ~15 minutes. Pericentrin and γ-tubulin form microtubule-nucleating units that are clustered by pericentrin self-association and assembled by dynein-based transport, with CDK5RAP2 contributing to nucleation efficiency and ninein to cluster compaction.
evaluation: Claims C127-C145 are supported by time-course experiments after nocodazole washout (Figures 5A-G, Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2) including immunofluorescence at multiple timepoints, live cell imaging, and systematic protein depletion studies. The temporal sequence of protein recruitment and the differential effects of depleting specific proteins provide strong evidence for the proposed assembly mechanism.

result: In AKAP450 knockout cells, CAMSAP2-stabilized microtubule minus ends are randomly distributed and relatively stationary, forming a disorganized network. Small pericentrin-dependent PCM clusters move along these microtubules in random directions driven by dynein, but do not coalesce into a single caMTOC because the disorganized microtubule network prevents convergent transport.
evaluation: Claims C146-C156 are supported by live cell imaging (Figure 6A-B, Videos 4-7), immunofluorescence (Figure 6A), and dynein inhibitor experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-E). The data show that CAMSAP2-decorated minus ends have limited motility while PCM clusters move randomly, and pericentrin depletion eliminates PCM clustering, supporting the mechanistic interpretation.

result: Linking CAMSAP2 to the minus-end-directed motor ppKin14 through inducible heterodimerization leads to radial microtubule organization in >90% of cells after 2 hours, with CAMSAP2-bound minus ends forming either a tight cluster or a whirlpool-like ring in the cell center. Major caMTOC components (pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, γ-tubulin, ninein) concentrate within the CAMSAP2 cluster, demonstrating that positioning of stabilized minus-ends is an important determinant of microtubule organization and PCM localization.
evaluation: Claims C19, C157-C161 are supported by the heterodimerization experiments (Figures 6D-G) showing recruitment of ppKin14 to CAMSAP2, quantification of microtubule organization (>90% radial, n=385 cells), and colocalization of PCM components. The experimental design provides a direct test of the hypothesis that minus-end positioning controls MTOC formation.

result: In AKAP450/CAMSAP2/p53/pericentrin knockout cells, linking CAMSAP2 to ppKin14 produces radial microtubule organization but minus ends accumulate in a 30-70 μm ring-like structure rather than a compact cluster. Transient transfection with GFP-pericentrin rescues tight CAMSAP2 cluster formation, demonstrating that pericentrin-containing self-clustering PCM is required for MTOC compaction and that coupling stable minus-ends to a minus-end-directed motor alone is insufficient.
evaluation: Claims C20, C162-C171 are supported by experiments in pericentrin knockout cells (Figures 7A-D) showing ring-like CAMSAP2 organization and rescue experiments with GFP-pericentrin (Figure 7C). The comparison between cells with and without pericentrin provides strong evidence that PCM self-association is required for compact MTOC formation beyond motor-driven transport.

result: Computer simulations using Cytosim show that 300 PCM complexes with adhesive interactions form a compact central cluster through dynein-mediated positive feedback, requiring approximately 150 complexes for robust clustering. Disabling adhesive interactions produces ring-like arrangements. A stationary randomly organized microtubule network (300 immobile microtubules with only 50 of 300 PCM complexes nucleating) disrupts clustering, but increasing adhesive interaction strength restores it. These predictions are validated by experimental induction of pericentrin homodimerization.
evaluation: Claims C173-C185 are supported by systematic computational simulations (Figure 8A-D, Videos 9A-D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1) with parameter variations and quantification of cluster properties. The simulations recapitulate experimental observations and make testable predictions. The pericentrin homodimerization experiment (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) validates the simulation predictions about adhesive interaction strength.

result: Simulations of CAMSAP-kin14 complexes (300 non-adhesive complexes) produce loose ring-like arrangements, but introducing adhesive interactions promotes compact cluster formation. In mixed systems with 150 CAMSAP-kin14 and 150 adhesive PCM complexes, a compact central cluster forms with both complex types mixed, but making PCM non-adhesive prevents compaction. At least half of microtubules must be attached to adhesive PCM components for compaction to occur.
evaluation: Claims C186-C191 are supported by simulations (Figures 8G-L, Videos 9I-J, Figure 8—figure supplement 1G) showing the effects of adhesive interactions in CAMSAP-kin14 systems and mixed systems. The quantitative threshold (≥50% adhesive PCM) is determined through systematic parameter variation. These results align with experimental observations in pericentrin knockout cells.

result: FRAP experiments show that GFP-CDK5RAP2 in caMTOCs displays very slow and incomplete fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, with highly condensed caMTOCs showing largely immobile components and more loosely organized caMTOCs showing some rearrangement. This indicates caMTOCs display variable degrees of compaction and limited exchange with the cytoplasmic pool.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by FRAP data (Figures 1H-I) showing quantified recovery curves for different bleaching conditions (whole vs. partial). The interpretation that components are largely immobile is reasonable given the slow, incomplete recovery, though the alternative explanation that most GFP-CDK5RAP2 is accumulated within the caMTOC is speculative.

result: PLK4 depletion by siRNA produces caMTOCs similar to PLK4 inhibition with centrinone B, indicating catalytically inactive PLK4 has no scaffolding role. CPAP depletion is less efficient at inducing caMTOCs than PLK4 depletion, but centrinone B treatment of CPAP-depleted cells promotes caMTOC assembly. PLK1 inhibition with BI2536 has no effect on caMTOC formation.
evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are supported by systematic comparison of different centriole removal methods (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-G) with quantification of PCM organization types. The data show differential efficiency of CPAP vs. PLK4 depletion and rescue by centrinone B, supporting the conclusion about PLK4's catalytic role. However, incomplete protein depletion by siRNA is a limitation.

result: EB1 and EB3 are not enriched within caMTOCs, and caMTOCs can form in cells lacking EB3, CAMSAP2, the C-terminal partner-binding half of EB1, and AKAP450, indicating that the core +TIP machinery is not required for caMTOC formation.
evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by immunofluorescence showing lack of EB1/EB3 enrichment (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 5A) and caMTOC formation in EB1/EB3 mutant cells (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 5B-C). This is a clear negative result with appropriate controls.

result: Interphase PCM contains components that can self-assemble into a compact structure and organize microtubules, but PCM self-organization is sensitive to motor- and microtubule-based rearrangement. Self-association of interphase PCM is strong enough to promote clustering but sufficiently dynamic to allow reorganization dependent on other microtubule regulators.
evaluation: Claims C21, C22, C172 represent overarching conclusions drawn from the entire body of experimental and computational work. These conclusions are well-supported by the collective evidence from caMTOC formation, disassembly/reassembly dynamics, CAMSAP2 experiments, pericentrin requirements, and simulations. The claims appropriately synthesize the major findings.
